title: The Full AI Coding Tool Landscape

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll have a complete map of every AI coding tool covered in this course, a decision matrix for choosing between them, and a personal reference card you've written yourself — the one you'll actually use.

## You've Covered a Lot of Ground

Parts 6 through 9 covered eight AI coding tools. That's a lot to hold in your head. Before we move on to automation and APIs, let's step back and make sense of the whole landscape.

Here is every tool, with its honest positioning:

**GitHub Copilot** — The market leader. Best-in-class inline completions. Deep VS Code and JetBrains integration. Free tier available. The default choice for most developers.

**Continue.dev** — Open source, works with any model. Ideal if you want Claude-quality completions without a Copilot subscription, or want to use a local model.

**Cursor** — AI-native editor built on VS Code. The best tool for complex multi-file edits where you want AI to understand the whole project and make larger changes.

**Windsurf** — Cursor competitor with a different interface style. Acquired by Cognition (maker of the Devin agent) in mid-2025; its signature Cascade agent is being retired in 2026 and folded into Cognition's Devin product line. Worth knowing, but treat it as a tool in active transition rather than a stable standalone product.

**Claude Code** — The tool you've been using throughout this course. An agentic CLI that can read, plan, and edit entire projects. Best for whole-project tasks, MCP integrations, and when you want AI that can reason about architecture.

**Aider** — Terminal-based, git-native. Every edit becomes a commit. Best when you want a clean, auditable AI edit history and a focused workflow.

**Cody** — VS Code extension designed for large codebases. Best at cross-file understanding. The right tool when you need to ask "how does this all fit together?" on a project with hundreds of files.

**Tabnine** — Privacy-first completions. Can run entirely locally. The correct choice for regulated industries and environments where code can't leave the machine.

## Beyond These Eight: Other Tools You'll Hear About

The eight tools above are the ones worth learning hands-on in this course — but the landscape is bigger, and new entrants keep changing the competitive picture. Worth knowing about, even without a dedicated lesson:

**Devin (Cognition)** — A cloud-based autonomous coding agent, not an editor: you file a ticket, it plans and executes the work, and you review the resulting pull request. Best on scoped, well-defined tasks (dependency upgrades, test generation, bug fixes); open-ended architecture work still needs a human driving. As noted above, Windsurf has been folded into Devin's product line rather than continuing as a separate editor.

**Zed** — An open-source, AI-native code editor with full "bring your own model" support, meaning you can connect it to Claude, GPT, a local model, or any other provider rather than being locked into one vendor's models the way Claude Code, Codex, and Devin currently are.

**Warp 2.0** — A terminal built around agentic workflows, now a serious CLI competitor alongside Claude Code and Codex CLI for developers who live in the terminal.

**Amazon Q Developer** — An IDE-extension-style assistant (like Copilot) that's specifically strong for AWS-centric infrastructure and DevOps work, since it understands AWS's own cloud primitives more natively than general-purpose tools.

**OpenCode** — A model-agnostic, fully open-source CLI agent that has grown into one of the most-starred projects in this space — a sign of how much developer interest there is in tools that aren't locked to one company's models.

The pattern holds regardless of which specific names are current when you're reading this: most experienced developers don't pick one tool for everything. A common setup is an agentic CLI (Claude Code, Codex CLI) for complex multi-file work, an in-editor assistant (Copilot, Cline, Zed) for daily completions, and an autonomous cloud agent (Devin) for well-scoped batch tasks — three different tools for three different shapes of work, not one tool trying to do everything.

## Decision Matrix

Use this table as a starting point. Fill in your own scores as you try each tool.

| Tool | Best for | Cost | Privacy | Works offline |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GitHub Copilot | Daily completions, general coding | Free tier / $10/mo | Cloud (Microsoft) | No |
| Continue.dev | Free Claude completions, model flexibility | Free (OSS) | Configurable | Yes (with Ollama) |
| Cursor | Complex multi-file edits, AI-first workflow | Free tier / $20/mo | Some telemetry | No |
| Windsurf | Alternative to Cursor (now part of Cognition/Devin) | Free tier / $20/mo | Codeium/Cognition cloud | No |
| Claude Code | Whole-project agentic work, MCP | Claude Pro / API usage | Anthropic cloud | No |
| Aider | Git-native edits, clean AI commit history | Free (OSS + API cost) | Depends on model | Yes (with local model) |
| Cody | Large codebase navigation and understanding | Enterprise only (custom quote) since 2025 | Sourcegraph cloud | No |
| Tabnine | Privacy-required environments, regulated industries | Enterprise only, ~$39+/mo since 2026 | Local mode available | Yes (local mode) |

Notice the pattern: every tool makes a tradeoff between capability and control. The most capable tools (Claude Code, Cursor) send the most context to the cloud. The most private tools (Tabnine local, Aider with Ollama) require more setup and run with smaller models.

**The meta-skill matters more than the tools.** The tools in this table will change. Copilot will add features. New tools will launch. Prices will shift. What won't change is the underlying skill: knowing how to evaluate a new AI coding tool. When the next one drops, you now know the questions to ask — model quality, context window size, multi-file editing capability, privacy model, IDE integration, pricing tier structure. You can assess any tool in 30 minutes.

## What to Watch Going Forward

The AI coding tool space is moving faster than almost any other software category. Here are the signals worth tracking:

**Model quality** — The underlying model matters more than the wrapper. When a tool upgrades to a better base model, its suggestions improve overnight. Check what model each tool is using, not just the tool itself.

**Context window size** — How much of your codebase can the tool "see" at once? Larger context windows mean better cross-file understanding. This number has grown dramatically in two years and will keep growing.

**Multi-file editing** — Can the tool edit three files at once based on one instruction? This is the line between "autocomplete" and "coding agent." Tools crossing this line are getting much more powerful.

**IDE integration depth** — Is AI embedded in the editor, or bolted on? Cursor and Windsurf are building toward AI-first editors. VS Code is adding AI features to an existing foundation. Both approaches have advantages.

**Pricing stability** — Several tools in this list have changed pricing structures in the last 12 months. Free tiers that exist today may change. Keep an eye on the business models, especially for tools you rely on.

**Consolidation** — There are currently more AI coding tools than the market will sustainably support. Expect acquisitions, pivots, and shutdowns over the next 2–3 years. The underlying workflows you've learned survive any individual tool.

## The Honest Prediction

In 2–3 years, the AI coding tool landscape will likely look different:

- Fewer standalone tools — the major IDE players (VS Code, JetBrains) will have absorbed most of the functionality that Copilot and Cody currently provide as extensions
- Cursor-style AI-native editors will either win a meaningful market share or be absorbed by larger players
- Local models will be capable enough to handle most routine completions without cloud calls — making privacy-first tools more competitive
- The distinction between "AI coding assistant" and "coding agent" will blur further

What stays constant: the ability to direct AI to write, refactor, debug, and understand code. That skill compounds. The student who finishes this course and uses these tools daily for a year will be dramatically more capable than one who doesn't — regardless of which specific tools are still standing.

sections.title: Build Your Personal AI Coding Reference Card
sections.content:
**Goal:** Write a personal reference card in `notes/ai-tools-guide.md` that answers the real scenarios you'll face. This is the document you'll actually consult when you're starting a new project or onboarding somewhere new.

**Open VS Code and create the file:**
```
notes/ai-tools-guide.md
```

**Fill in each section with your honest answer based on everything you've tried:**

```markdown
# My AI Coding Tool Guide

## For everyday coding — quick completions while I write
Tool: ___
Why I chose it: ___
Backup if it's unavailable: ___

## For a big refactor across multiple files
Tool: ___
Why: ___

## For understanding a large codebase I'm joining
Tool: ___
Why: ___

## For an environment where code can't leave the machine
Tool: ___
Why: ___

## For free with maximum model quality
Tool: ___
Why: ___

## My daily setup right now
Primary: ___
For chat/planning: ___
For agentic tasks: ___

## Tools I want to revisit in 6 months
-
-
```

**Do this properly.** Write real answers, not placeholders. This is the synthesis of four parts of the course.

When you're done, commit the file to git:
```bash
git add notes/ai-tools-guide.md
git commit -m "Add personal AI coding tool reference card"
```

**Accomplishment check:** You have a committed, personal reference document that reflects your actual experience with these tools — not a generic list, but *your* judgment. This is more valuable than any comparison article you'll find online.

sections.title: Workshop A — AI Tool Landscape Mapping
sections.content:
Map the complete AI coding tool landscape as it exists today.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** *"Create a comprehensive map of the AI coding tool landscape in 2026. Include: in-editor assistants, terminal/CLI agents, AI-native IDEs, local models, and code review tools. For each category, name the leading tools."*

**Step 2 — Draw your personal landscape:** On paper or a diagram tool, place each tool you've encountered in this course in the right category.

**Step 3 — For each tool**, mark:
- ✓ Used (have hands-on experience)
- ~ Tried (briefly tested)
- ? Heard of (no experience)
- ✗ Not relevant to my work

**Step 4 — Identify your gaps:** Which tools are relevant to your work but marked ? — and what would it take to evaluate them?

**Step 5 — Ask Claude:** "Based on my current tool usage [describe it], what important AI coding tools am I missing that would significantly improve my workflow?"

sections.title: Workshop B — Build Your Optimal AI Coding Stack
sections.content:
Design your personal AI coding stack — the combination of tools you will actually use.

**Step 1 — List your current AI coding tools** (from Part 5-9 of this course).

**Step 2 — For each of your top 5 coding task types**, identify which tool is best:
| Task | Best Tool | Why |
|---|---|---|
| New feature implementation | | |
| Code review | | |
| Debugging | | |
| Documentation | | |
| Learning a new library | | |

**Step 3 — Identify gaps:** Are there task types that no current tool covers well?

**Step 4 — Ask Claude:** *"Review my AI coding stack [paste your table]. What tools are redundant? What gaps exist? What would a senior developer in [your field] add or remove?"*

**Step 5 — Finalise your stack** and commit to using it consistently for 60 days before evaluating.

sections.title: Workshop C — AI Tool Evaluation Framework
sections.content:
Build a framework for evaluating any new AI coding tool.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** *"Design an evaluation framework for AI coding tools. What criteria should I assess to decide whether to add a new tool to my workflow? Weight each criterion by importance."*

**Step 2 — Review the framework.** Add any criteria specific to your context (privacy requirements, team standardisation, cost constraints).

**Step 3 — Apply the framework** to a tool you haven't tried yet. Fill in each criterion with your best estimate.

**Step 4 — Set a decision threshold:** "I will add this tool to my stack if it scores above X across criteria Y, Z, and W."

**Step 5 — Save the framework.** Use it every time you're considering a new AI coding tool.

sections.title: Workshop D — AI Coding Skills Inventory and Growth Plan
sections.content:
Assess where you are in AI coding skills and plan your next development.

**Step 1 — Rate yourself (1-5) on these AI coding skills:**
- Using AI for code generation
- Reviewing AI-generated code effectively
- Prompting AI for debugging
- Using Claude Code for autonomous tasks
- Configuring MCP servers
- Building CLAUDE.md for projects
- Using custom slash commands
- Understanding when NOT to use AI

**Step 2 — Ask Claude:** *"Based on these self-ratings [paste yours], what are my 3 most impactful development areas? What resources or practice would improve each one most efficiently?"*

**Step 3 — Create a 90-day growth plan:** Specific practice activities for your top 3 development areas.

**Step 4 — Mandatory review:** Ask Claude: *"Review my growth plan. What are the most common mistakes people make when trying to improve in AI coding? What should I watch out for?"*

**Step 5 — Schedule monthly reviews** of your progress against the plan.

sections.question: You've evaluated 5 AI coding tools and they all perform similarly on your main tasks. What should be the tiebreaker?
options: Choose the most popular one — community size means more support
Choose the one that integrates best with your existing workflow and requires the least context switching
Choose the most expensive one — higher price typically means higher quality
Choose the newest one — it will have the latest technology
sections.explanation: When tools are functionally equivalent, workflow integration is the tiebreaker. The best tool is the one you'll actually use consistently — and consistency comes from low friction. A slightly less capable tool that's integrated into your existing workflow will deliver more value than a marginally better tool that requires significant context switching. Evaluate: does it fit where you already are, or does it require building new habits around it?

sections.question: The AI coding tool landscape changes rapidly with new tools releasing monthly. What is the right approach to staying current?
options: Constantly switch to the newest tool to stay at the cutting edge
Establish a stable core stack and evaluate new tools quarterly with your framework — don't switch unless a new tool offers meaningfully better value for your specific use cases
Ignore new tools until they've been out for at least 2 years
Follow social media recommendations and switch when a tool trends
sections.explanation: Constant switching prevents you from developing deep proficiency with any single tool — you never learn the shortcuts, the edge cases, or the best practices. A quarterly evaluation cadence balances staying current with building expertise. When evaluating, use your criteria framework (from Workshop C) and compare new tools to your current stack on your actual tasks, not benchmark comparisons. Only switch if the improvement is meaningful and consistent.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 9-4.** You've covered GitHub Copilot, Cody, and Tabnine and have a mental model for when each AI coding assistant fits best. Next: lessons 9-5 through 9-7 cover vibe coding tools — Bolt.new, v0.dev, Lovable, and Replit — that let you build full apps with AI without deep coding.
